label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Why I'm not dropping the busing project

Some of you have already heard about this, and a few of you have had opinions, which is fine. Jess texted me last night, and she was basically saying, "It's one assignment. Don't torch your job over it." Half the group chat agreed with her. I'd rather explain myself once, properly, than try to do it in fifteen texts, so this is that. It's really for Jess, but it's for everyone else too.

I'm not mad at her. I get why she said it. She knows how these things can go, and she knows what it's like to have a principal who controls your schedule. Her worry is a real one. I'm not writing this to win an argument with her. I want her to understand why I'm not going to back down, even if she still thinks I'm being stubborn.

Here's the situation. I teach juniors in US History II at Cobb Street High, two sections. The project is an oral history. Each student interviews someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston in 1974 to 1976, when busing and desegregation were tearing the city apart. They record a ten-minute interview and write a two-page reflection. I've run it for four years. Nobody has ever complained about it, not once, until this fall.

Now a parent has sent an email to Dr. Halvorsen, with a school committee member copied. The email says the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." Halvorsen wants to meet about it. That meeting is Thursday, November 19, at 3:15, with the parent. And the request, which has been made in a few different ways, is that I quietly drop the project and move on.

I'm not going to quietly drop it. But I also don't want to pretend this is simple, because it isn't.

I want to say something about the parent's concern, because I don't think it's crazy. The parent is right that the project asks a lot of kids. Some of them come from families where the subject is painful, and some of those families never talked about it at all. Asking a fifteen-year-old to sit down with a grandparent and ask what happened in 1974 is not a small thing. It can open doors the kid wasn't ready to open, or the grandparent wasn't ready to open. I actually think that's a fair point, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise when I sit down with her on Thursday.

Here's where I land, though. I've seen what happens when the project goes well, and I've seen what happens when it's hard. Both matter.

Two years ago, a kid I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about what happened on those routes. D. came in with his recording and asked if he could play a bit of it for the class. He played about forty seconds. Then nobody said anything for about a minute. I've taught a long time, and I can count on one hand the moments when a room went that quiet. That was a room full of seventeen-year-olds realizing this wasn't a textbook. This was somebody's grandmother, in the car they'd been reading about, telling the truth about it.

Last year a girl found out, during her interview, that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus when he was a teenager. She was upset. Really upset. We talked after class twice. She wasn't mad at me. She was mad at the situation, and at her uncle, and at herself for being surprised by it. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. She wrote about the difference between the story her family told and the one she'd just heard, and she didn't resolve it neatly, and she didn't pretend to. It was honest in a way I rarely get from anyone, let alone a junior.

That's the thing I keep coming back to. The kids who feel uncomfortable with this project are sometimes the ones who need it most. Not always. But often. The textbook gives the busing crisis one paragraph. For most of my students, that paragraph is the whole story. Yet this happened on the streets they walk on. Some of their parents and grandparents were in those neighborhoods. Some of them probably have a relative who was on one side or the other. If they never ask about it, the history doesn't go away. It just sits there in the family, unspoken.

But I also don't get to force anyone. That's the line for me, and I'm holding it. That's why I'm adding an alternate option. A student can interview a librarian or archivist, or use the recorded interviews from past years, with permission from the people who gave them. Nobody has to interview their own family. If a kid or a parent says no, that's a real answer, and it doesn't cost the kid a grade. If the parent in this complaint wants that protection written into the project, she gets it. The project stays, but the choice belongs to the kid.

I'm not trying to make this about her. I'm not picking a fight with the parent. I think she's worried about her kid, and she has a point about pressure, and I'd rather fix the pressure than fight about whether the history should be taught.

And I'll be honest about how I feel. I'm scared, a little. I'm tenured, since 2021, which helps, but Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP sections. I know what it looks like when a teacher gets labeled a problem. I've watched it happen to other people. So no, I'm not feeling especially brave. I'm feeling stubborn and worried at the same time, and I'm choosing to act on the first one.

Jess, I think you're right that I could get burned. I just don't think keeping quiet is safe in the way people assume. If I drop the project, I'm telling every kid in those two sections that the story of their own city is too uncomfortable to ask about. I'm not willing to say that to them.

So that's where I am. I'll sit down with Halvorsen and the parent on the 19th. I'll listen. I'll bring the alternate option and the changes I'm willing to make. And I'll keep the project.

I'll text you Thursday after the meeting, whatever happens. Even if it goes badly, I'd rather you hear it from me than from the group chat.
